questions.explanation: Fire risk is highest when oxygen collects under drapes near an ignition source during head and neck procedures.

questions.stem: TEE and synchronized cardioversion are examples of what procedural group commonly managed with carefully selected sedation techniques?
questions.explanation: TEE, selected cardiac catheterizations, and cardioversion are short cardiovascular procedures often done under sedation when appropriate.

questions.stem: A patient with severe COPD, predicted difficult airway, and esophageal food impaction is scheduled for EGD. Which principle should determine MAC versus a secured airway?
options: Use MAC because EGD is usually performed under sedation
Choose solely according to patient preference
Integrate aspiration risk, airway rescue difficulty, comorbidity, and procedural requirements rather than relying on the usual anesthetic for EGD
questions.explanation: A procedure that is usually done under sedation is appropriate only when the airway, comorbidities, complexity, and stimulation allow it. This patient may need GA with a protected airway.

questions.stem: A percutaneous biopsy carries meaningful hemorrhage risk. How should that risk affect sedation planning?
options: Ensure monitoring/access and a plan for sudden hemodynamic deterioration or escalation of care
It eliminates the need for airway planning
It guarantees general anesthesia is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Bleeding risk means sudden hemodynamic changes may occur, which shapes monitoring and readiness to convert.

questions.stem: Why is shoulder-dislocation reduction often well suited to brief deep sedation in an appropriately selected patient?
options: The stimulus is intense but short, and rapid recovery is desirable
The patient must follow commands throughout reduction
questions.explanation: Joint reductions are short and intensely stimulating, and patients need to recover quickly afterward.

questions.stem: During beach-chair MAC, arm BP falls to 85/50 mmHg. Which concern should drive prompt reassessment and treatment?
options: The main risk is prone airway edema
Cerebral perfusion at head level may be even lower than the arm pressure indicates
Blood pressure is irrelevant if SpO2 is normal
questions.explanation: In the upright beach-chair position, arterial pressure at brain level may be lower than an arm-cuff measurement because of the hydrostatic gradient. Promptly reassess the measurement reference and treat clinically important hypotension to protect cerebral perfusion.

questions.stem: During shoulder surgery, the patient's head is turned away and airway access is partly obstructed by the setup. What risk increases if sedation deepens?
options: Elimination of the need for capnography
Delay or difficulty performing airway rescue
questions.explanation: Head-away positioning makes airway access difficult, which increases the danger if sedation becomes deeper than intended.

questions.stem: Which procedural combination most strongly argues against deep sedation with an unsecured airway?
options: Intense variable stimulation plus poor airway access and inability to pause quickly
Low stimulation with easy airway access
Short duration with a cooperative patient
A procedure that can be stopped immediately
questions.explanation: Prone or otherwise restricted positioning can turn a minor airway problem into an emergency because the face and airway may be difficult to reach quickly. The sedation plan must account for access before dosing begins and establish how oxygenation, ventilation, and airway control will be restored if obstruction occurs.

questions.stem: Which FIVE factors matter when deciding whether a long interventional-radiology case is suitable for sedation? (Select 5)
options: Availability of a particular PACU nurse
questions.explanation: Duration, immobility, airway position, bleeding and aspiration risk, stimulation, ability to interrupt, and cooperation all shape procedure selection.

questions.stem: Late in a prolonged MAC, a previously comfortable patient becomes restless. What should occur before simply escalating sedative doses?
options: Assume restlessness always means inadequate hypnosis
Evaluate reversible causes such as pain, position, bladder discomfort, hypoxemia, or inadequate local anesthesia because extra sedative may cause airway compromise
Give repeated propofol boluses until immobile
questions.explanation: Long cases make patients restless, which prompts more drug and raises the chance of deeper-than-intended sedation. Consider whether discomfort, position, or a full bladder is the real cause.

questions.stem: Deep sedation is requested for a prone patient whose airway would be difficult to access. What is the safest planning response?
options: Proceed because pulse oximetry will identify problems early enough
Reconsider whether a secured airway/general anesthetic offers a safer rescue profile
Assume the patient can be rapidly turned supine during any emergency
questions.explanation: Prone positioning makes airway access difficult. A secured airway or GA may be safer than deep sedation.

questions.stem: A laterally positioned patient under MAC develops mild hypoxemia. Which mechanical change can contribute?
options: Improved oxygen reserve in both lungs
Reduced FRC/compliance in the dependent lung
questions.explanation: In the lateral position, the dependent lung loses compliance and FRC, worsening gas exchange.

questions.stem: Why is postoperative visual loss emphasized despite its low incidence after prolonged prone surgery?
options: The injury is rare but potentially permanent and devastating
It is common but always reversible
It occurs mainly after brief supine cases
It is caused only by direct eye pressure
questions.explanation: Postoperative visual loss is rare but can be permanent, which is why prevention matters.

questions.stem: Which common procedure most often pairs a very brief but intense stimulus with a need for rapid recovery?
options: Superficial abscess drainage with adequate local anesthesia
questions.explanation: Cardioversion is usually brief deep sedation because the shock is intensely stimulating. The others are usually manageable at lighter depths.

questions.stem: During colonoscopy under deep sedation, forceful external abdominal pressure is applied while protective reflexes are depressed. Which risk may increase?
questions.explanation: External abdominal pressure can push gastric contents upward while the airway is unprotected.

questions.stem: When planning procedural sedation, which question best predicts peak analgesic requirement?
options: What oxygen flow rate will be used?
How many staff are in the room?
How intense and variable will the noxious stimulation be?
questions.explanation: The intensity and variability of stimulation determine how much sedation and analgesia are needed.

questions.stem: Why can carpal-tunnel release often be performed with effective local anesthesia and only minimal systemic sedation?
options: Adequate local anesthesia can blunt the procedural nociceptive input, reducing the need for systemic drugs
The procedure requires intense variable stimulation despite local anesthesia
The airway is shared with the surgeon
questions.explanation: Effective local anesthesia makes stimulation low, so minimal sedation is enough.

questions.stem: Why does MRI sedation demand special rescue planning even though the scan itself is painless?
options: The remote environment, scanner bore, and MRI-compatibility constraints can delay physical access and airway rescue
Monitoring is unnecessary because no incision occurs
questions.explanation: MRI suites are remote, the bore limits airway access, and only MRI-compatible equipment can be used, which slows rescue.

questions.stem: A supine patient with severe OSA repeatedly obstructs during sedation. Which positional adjustment may improve upper-airway patency if the procedure permits?
questions.explanation: Supine positioning lets the tongue and soft tissue fall back, worsening OSA obstruction. Lateral or semi-upright positions improve airway patency.

questions.stem: During sedated TEE, hypoxemia develops and airway maneuvers are difficult. Which procedural factor contributes directly?
options: The patient must perform neurologic testing
The probe occupies the pharyngeal space and may impede airway access until withdrawn
questions.explanation: During TEE, the probe occupies the pharynx and esophagus, limiting airway access; it may need to be removed to manage the airway.

questions.stem: A procedure alternates between minimal stimulation and brief intense pain. What is the principal titration challenge?
options: Drug effect may outlast the painful stimulus, causing oversedation when stimulation suddenly falls
The deepest required level should be maintained throughout
Changing stimulation affects analgesia but never sedation depth
questions.explanation: Local or regional anesthesia reduces nociceptive input but does not guarantee patient tolerance, immobility, or airway safety. Sedation still requires titration to the patient's response, and the team must remain prepared for block failure, increasing stimulation, or conversion to general anesthesia.

questions.stem: During beach-chair MAC, a patient becomes confused with arm BP 92/54 mmHg. Which explanation should be considered urgently?
options: Upright positioning guarantees adequate cerebral perfusion
Cerebral perfusion pressure at head level may be inadequate despite the arm-cuff value
Dependent-lung collapse is the only likely cause
Direct eye pressure is causing the confusion
questions.explanation: Confusion during beach-chair positioning should prompt urgent evaluation of cerebral perfusion and other causes. If pressure is measured at the arm, the hydrostatic gradient can make pressure at brain level lower than the displayed cuff value.

questions.stem: Why must position be considered during MAC even when no airway device is planned?
options: Position matters only during general anesthesia
Position can alter airway patency, rescue access, ventilation, and perfusion
questions.explanation: Position affects airway patency, access for rescue, and physiology such as cerebral perfusion and FRC.

questions.stem: A lateral-position patient under MAC develops mild desaturation without obvious obstruction. Which positional physiology may contribute?
questions.explanation: Lateral positioning lowers FRC and compliance in the dependent lung, reducing oxygen reserve.

questions.stem: A patient in steep Trendelenburg for prolonged robotic surgery develops marked facial and conjunctival edema. Which emergence concern should this finding raise most directly?
options: Potential upper-airway edema and difficult extubation
The patient no longer needs neuromuscular monitoring
questions.explanation: Prolonged steep Trendelenburg can produce facial and upper-airway edema. Marked external edema should prompt reassessment of airway swelling and extubation readiness rather than being used as a specific diagnosis of postoperative visual loss.

questions.stem: Why is it incorrect to treat MAC as a fixed depth between moderate and deep sedation?
options: MAC is synonymous with deep sedation
MAC describes an anesthesia service and preparedness, not a single sedation depth
questions.explanation: MAC describes a service by an anesthesia professional and can range from minimal sedation to GA. Depth does not define it.

questions.stem: During a case planned as MAC, a propofol bolus makes the patient unresponsive to painful stimulation and ventilation requires support. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: The event automatically becomes nurse-administered moderate sedation
The patient remains at moderate sedation because the case was booked as MAC
The patient has entered general anesthesia depth and must be managed/rescued accordingly; documentation and anesthetic classification should reflect the actual care delivered
Airway intervention is incompatible with MAC preparedness
questions.explanation: MAC describes a planned anesthesia service, not a guaranteed depth. If the patient becomes unarousable even to painful stimulation, the physiologic depth is general anesthesia and must be managed accordingly. Billing/documentation terminology should reflect the actual anesthetic care rather than implying that a MAC label overrides the observed depth.

questions.stem: Why is credentialing for nurse-administered moderate sedation not equivalent to providing MAC?
options: Moderate-sedation credentials automatically authorize general anesthesia
Both roles are identical if propofol is not used
MAC is an anesthesia service requiring an anesthesia professional prepared for deeper anesthesia, airway rescue, and conversion to general anesthesia
questions.explanation: MAC is a specific anesthesia service furnished by a qualified anesthesia professional who performs a preanesthetic evaluation, provides intra-procedure anesthesia care, and is prepared to rescue the airway or convert the anesthetic when necessary. Scope and credentialing for non-anesthesia moderate sedation are governed separately.

questions.stem: Which THREE components are part of the MAC anesthesia service? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: MAC includes preprocedure evaluation, intraprocedure care, and postprocedure management, the same scope as other anesthetics.

questions.stem: Which medication strategy can be part of MAC when appropriate to the procedure and patient?
options: A tailored combination of anxiolytic, hypnotic, analgesic, and/or amnestic drugs with local/regional anesthesia as applicable
Neuromuscular blockade solely to keep an unsecured-airway patient still
Benzodiazepines and opioids are the only permissible agents
questions.explanation: MAC may use anxiolytic, hypnotic, analgesic, and amnestic drugs, alone or with local or regional anesthesia.

questions.stem: During MAC, a field block fails; severe pain persists, and attempts to deepen sedation repeatedly cause obstruction. What should the anesthesia provider be prepared to do?
options: Continue escalating propofol despite recurrent obstruction
Change the anesthetic plan, including conversion to general anesthesia with a secured airway when needed
Use neuromuscular blockade without securing the airway
Ignore pain until the procedure ends
questions.explanation: MAC requires readiness to convert to GA when the procedure cannot proceed safely, as with a failed block and obstruction.

questions.stem: A facility proposes skipping the airway assessment because a patient is scheduled for MAC rather than general anesthesia. What is the key flaw?
options: MAC cannot progress to general anesthesia
Airway assessment is relevant only when intubation is planned
MAC requires preanesthetic evaluation and readiness for airway rescue/conversion because depth can change
Only the proceduralist needs to assess the airway
questions.explanation: Because MAC can progress to GA, its evaluation and monitoring standards are comparable to GA, including the airway exam.

questions.stem: Absolute immobility is required for a procedure despite adequate analgesia. Which capability can general anesthesia provide that routine MAC cannot safely guarantee?
options: Controlled immobility including neuromuscular blockade with a secured anesthetic plan when indicated
questions.explanation: A change in procedure duration or invasiveness can invalidate the original MAC plan by increasing pain, immobility requirements, drug exposure, or loss of airway access. Reassessment should occur before simply escalating sedation, because conversion to a secured general anesthetic may become the safer technique.

questions.stem: What fundamentally distinguishes intended moderate sedation from an anesthesia-provider MAC service?
options: Moderate sedation targets preserved purposeful responsiveness, whereas MAC is a broader anesthesia service prepared for changing depth and rescue/conversion
MAC is always deeper than moderate sedation
Moderate sedation requires an anesthesia professional in every case
MAC excludes local or regional anesthesia
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation keeps purposeful response; MAC can go deeper and includes readiness to convert to GA.

questions.stem: During an otherwise stable MAC, the anesthesia professional leaves the room and the patient becomes apneic. Which principle was violated?
options: Presence only during induction and emergence
Continuous anesthesia-team vigilance/presence appropriate to the anesthetic
Presence only after conversion to general anesthesia
Presence only for ASA IV patients
questions.explanation: Anesthesia care requires continuous qualified vigilance. The key violation is leaving an anesthetized/sedated patient without appropriate anesthesia observation and rescue capability; depth can change rapidly.

questions.stem: Which item is NOT routinely required solely because a case is performed under MAC?
questions.explanation: MAC requirements include preanesthesia evaluation, a qualified provider, continuous monitoring, airway management, conversion to GA, and postanesthesia care. Arterial lines depend on the patient.

questions.stem: Which FIVE elements belong in a safe MAC system? (Select 5)
options: Readiness to convert to general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Safe MAC includes an appropriate preanesthetic evaluation and plan, a qualified anesthesia professional, continuous monitoring/vigilance, immediate rescue capability including conversion when necessary, and appropriate postanesthesia care. Volatile maintenance is not inherently required.

questions.stem: A MAC patient obstructs, but the room has only nasal oxygen and suction. What preparation was inadequate?
options: Nasal oxygen and suction are sufficient for obstruction
Every MAC patient should have been intubated initially
A code team should replace bedside rescue capability
Equipment and capability for positive-pressure ventilation and advanced airway rescue were not immediately available
questions.explanation: MAC requires immediate availability of airway equipment and the ability to provide ventilatory support.

questions.stem: After MAC, a drowsy patient is sent toward discharge without monitored recovery or reassessment. What is missing?
options: Nothing if the patient can speak
questions.explanation: Sedation can deepen unexpectedly, and a patient who initially maintains the airway may later obstruct or become apneic. Effective MAC preparation therefore includes immediately available oxygen, suction, airway adjuncts, positive-pressure ventilation capability, and equipment and drugs for conversion to general anesthesia.

questions.stem: A MAC preoperative note lists NPO status and allergies but omits severe OSA, GERD, medications, and prior difficult intubation. Which deficiency is most important?
options: A routine chest radiograph is missing
The evaluation failed to characterize airway, aspiration, medication, and comorbidity risks that could alter rescue planning
A routine stress test is missing
The surgeon's preferred sedative is missing
questions.explanation: The MAC preanesthesia evaluation includes history, medications, allergies, airway, and aspiration risk; this patient's OSA, GERD, and airway history are critical.

questions.stem: A continuous propofol technique is planned, but no reliable infusion pump is available. What is the best response?
options: Estimate the infusion by counting drops
Obtain appropriate controlled-infusion equipment or change to a safely deliverable anesthetic plan
Proceed because propofol dose precision is unnecessary during MAC
questions.explanation: Infusion pumps are part of the MAC environment when continuous agents are used; gravity delivery is unreliable.

questions.stem: Why does a remote procedure room with imaging equipment blocking the head increase MAC risk?
options: It decreases the need for rescue equipment
Restricted physical access can delay airway maneuvers and conversion to a secured airway
questions.explanation: Workspace and equipment can limit airway access, especially in remote locations.

questions.stem: A high-risk TAVR is planned under MAC. Why must the person providing the anesthetic have advanced airway and general-anesthesia rescue capability?
options: MAC can deepen unexpectedly or require rapid conversion because of patient/procedural deterioration
Only cardiovascular procedures require rescue capability
Moderate-sedation credentials are equivalent to MAC training
questions.explanation: MAC is provided by an anesthesia provider capable of airway rescue and converting to GA.

questions.stem: A patient remains lightly sedated and conversational throughout a procedure managed by an anesthesia professional as MAC. Why can the service still be MAC?
options: MAC is defined by the anesthesia service and preparedness, not a required depth
MAC requires loss of verbal responsiveness
MAC requires general anesthesia at some point
questions.explanation: MAC describes the anesthesia service provided, not how deep the patient is.

questions.stem: Which scenario most clearly represents MAC?
options: A procedural nurse administers protocolized moderate sedation
An anesthesia professional manages the anesthetic with full monitoring and readiness for airway rescue/conversion
A proceduralist gives sedative while simultaneously performing the procedure
questions.explanation: MAC is delivered by an anesthesia provider with readiness to convert to GA.

questions.stem: During MAC, coughing, agitation, and movement make the procedure unsafe despite attempts to correct reversible causes. What should the anesthesia professional be prepared to do?
options: Finish the procedure before changing the anesthetic
Wait for the surgeon alone to decide whether airway rescue is needed
Change the anesthetic plan, including conversion to general anesthesia when clinically necessary
questions.explanation: ASA requires readiness to convert to GA whenever it is clinically necessary.

questions.stem: A remote endoscopy room lacks capnography, positive-pressure ventilation equipment, and emergency drugs. Which THREE deficiencies must be corrected before anesthesia-provider MAC? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The MAC environment requires oxygen, suction, ventilation equipment, physiologic monitoring with capnography, emergency drugs, and airway equipment.

questions.stem: During cataract MAC, a patient briefly stops responding to voice after propofol but still responds purposefully to repeated tactile stimulation and ventilates adequately. What is the best interpretation?
options: The patient has deepened along the sedation continuum; the MAC service label does not replace assessment of the actual depth and physiology
Any loss of verbal response automatically means general anesthesia
The case becomes nurse-administered moderate sedation
Airway intervention can never be required during MAC
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen treats hypoxemia but does not correct upper-airway obstruction or inadequate alveolar ventilation. If capnography and clinical observation show apnea or obstruction, the airway and ventilation must be restored even when SpO2 remains temporarily normal.

questions.stem: Why should an airway assessment not be omitted simply because MAC rather than general anesthesia is planned?
options: Airway assessment is relevant only to ASA III–IV patients
Unintended deepening or procedural change may require immediate airway rescue or conversion
Airway assessment is needed only when deep sedation is planned
questions.explanation: Because any MAC patient may need conversion to GA, the preop evaluation should be as comprehensive as for GA.

questions.stem: Monitors and sedatives are ready for MAC, but no airway device, induction medications, or conversion strategy has been prepared. What is missing?
options: A preplanned pathway for conversion to general anesthesia
A plan for routine neuromuscular blockade
questions.explanation: A conversion-to-GA plan with equipment and drugs must be developed before starting MAC.

questions.stem: Which FIVE factors can substantially increase risk during MAC? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Important MAC risk conditions include severe cardiovascular disease, pulmonary hypertension, OSA, morbid obesity, renal or hepatic disease, chronic opioid use, and advanced age.

questions.stem: Why does inability to tolerate the required position or duration increase risk during MAC?
options: Position tolerance affects only surgical exposure
Discomfort/restlessness may drive escalating sedation, increasing respiratory and airway risk
questions.explanation: If a patient cannot tolerate position or duration, she moves and becomes restless, which leads to deeper sedation with an unsecured airway. That may favor GA.

questions.stem: Which setup most compromises emergency airway access during MAC?
options: Prone positioning with the head turned away and partially inaccessible
Semi-upright with direct access to the head
Lateral with the face fully visible
questions.explanation: Prone positioning with the head turned away makes it hard to reach and manage the airway, so plan for loss of access.

questions.stem: A regional block is combined with titrated propofol sedation managed by an anesthesia professional with full rescue capability. How is the anesthesia service best described?
options: Regional anesthesia only because a block was placed
General anesthesia solely because propofol was used
Moderate sedation solely because the patient remained arousable
questions.explanation: MAC can be combined with local or regional anesthesia and is defined by the anesthesia service.

questions.stem: After light propofol MAC, a patient remains drowsy and intermittently hypoventilates. What should happen next?
options: Discharge once the patient can answer questions
Bypass recovery because the case was MAC
Continue appropriate monitored postanesthesia recovery until respiratory and discharge criteria are satisfied
Send directly home if no opioid was used
questions.explanation: MAC patients usually go to some form of PACU for monitoring and assessment, especially if they are still sedated.

questions.stem: A procedural sedation nurse and a CRNA use similar drugs. What most clearly distinguishes the CRNA's MAC service?
options: Achievement of deep sedation in every case
Anesthesia-level evaluation, monitoring, rescue capability, and readiness to convert to general anesthesia
questions.explanation: MAC is defined by the provider's qualification and readiness to convert to GA, not by the drugs or depth.

questions.stem: A prolonged MAC record shows ECG, SpO2, and NIBP but no ventilation monitoring; temperature is also omitted despite major exposure and heat-loss risk. Which elements are missing?
options: Ventilation monitoring and clinically indicated temperature monitoring
questions.explanation: Continuous monitoring during MAC includes oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature when indicated; a 4-hour case indicates temperature.

questions.stem: Why does a healthy patient still require a meaningful anesthesia preoperative evaluation before MAC?
options: MAC eliminates airway risk in healthy patients
The anesthetic can deepen or require conversion, so airway, aspiration, comorbidity, medication, and procedural risks still matter
Only ASA III–IV patients require preoperative evaluation
The evaluation is needed only for billing
questions.explanation: MAC can progress to GA at any time, so the evaluation must be comparable to GA.

questions.stem: A patient under MAC transiently reaches a deep anesthetic state. Which statement is correct?
options: MAC automatically ends at deep sedation
The provider must manage the actual depth appropriately; MAC itself describes the anesthesia service rather than a fixed depth
Depth no longer needs to be documented
questions.explanation: MAC is a specific anesthesia service for procedures, not a depth level.

questions.stem: Why are robust evaluation, monitoring, and rescue standards required during MAC?
options: MAC cases are always longer than general anesthetics
MAC patients are always high ASA status
The patient's depth and physiology can change unexpectedly, including progression requiring general-anesthesia rescue
questions.explanation: Because sedation can slide into GA without warning, MAC requires the same evaluation, monitoring, and presence standards as GA.

questions.stem: After MAC, a verbal handoff occurs but recovery vital signs and postanesthesia assessment are never documented. Which element is missing?
questions.explanation: ASA requires postanesthesia monitoring and documentation after MAC.

questions.stem: Adequate local anesthesia controls pain, but the patient is anxious about recalling the procedure. Which drug property may be useful as part of a balanced MAC technique?
questions.explanation: Amnestic drugs reduce recall during MAC; they do not provide analgesia or immobility.

questions.stem: Midazolam and fentanyl are titrated together for moderate sedation. What is the principal safety implication of this multimodal strategy?
options: Using two agents guarantees lighter sedation
Complementary effects may improve anxiolysis/analgesia but can synergistically depress ventilation
questions.explanation: Midazolam supplies anxiolysis, sedation, and amnesia while fentanyl supplies analgesia, so the combination can improve procedural tolerance. Both also depress ventilation, and together they can produce synergistic respiratory depression that is greater than expected from either dose alone.

questions.stem: A remote interventional-radiology suite lacks backup suction and capnography. What principle applies?
options: Backup suction is needed only for general anesthesia
Remote locations may omit respiratory monitoring
Pulse oximetry substitutes for capnography remotely
Anesthesia safety and rescue capability should not be reduced simply because the procedure occurs outside the main OR
questions.explanation: Anesthesia care in a remote location should provide monitoring, oxygenation/ventilation support, suction, emergency drugs, and rescue resources appropriate to the patient and anesthetic. Safety expectations do not become lower simply because the procedure is outside the main OR.

questions.stem: Which FIVE issues matter most before prolonged shoulder MAC in a frail patient with COPD and kyphosis? (Select 5)
options: Risk of obstruction or limited airway access
questions.explanation: The MAC preop assessment covers tolerance of position and duration, airway obstruction or loss of access, analgesic requirement, cooperation, and a conversion plan.

questions.stem: A patient with severe cardiovascular disease is scheduled for MAC. Which planning priority is most important?
options: Anticipate limited hemodynamic reserve and prepare monitoring, drugs, and conversion/rescue accordingly
Use lighter sedation so instability cannot occur
Plan inhaled induction regardless of procedure
questions.explanation: Severe cardiovascular disease is a listed risk condition. Planning for instability and conversion is essential.

questions.stem: During MAC, the patient becomes unresponsive to painful stimulation and ventilation becomes inadequate. What is the correct response?
options: Continue unchanged because the case is labeled MAC
Recognize general-anesthesia depth and immediately manage airway/ventilation while escalating the anesthetic plan as needed
Reclassify the patient as moderately sedated
Wait for spontaneous recovery before supporting ventilation
questions.explanation: MAC depth may range from minimal sedation to GA; the provider must be ready to manage the airway at any depth.

questions.stem: Which provider capability is essential for high-risk MAC such as TAVR?
options: An anesthesia professional able to manage major physiologic changes and rapidly rescue/convert the airway and anesthetic
questions.explanation: MAC must be provided by a qualified anesthesia provider.

questions.stem: Which statement about MAC and moderate sedation is incorrect?
options: Intended moderate sedation preserves purposeful responsiveness
They are identical services distinguished only by the drug chosen
questions.explanation: MAC and moderate sedation differ in provider, possible depth, and readiness to convert to GA.

questions.stem: Which developments commonly force conversion from MAC to general anesthesia?
options: Failed regional/local technique, inability to tolerate the procedure, or airway/oxygenation failure
Mild preoperative anxiety, brief nausea, or a single stable BP reading
Use of capnography, supplemental oxygen, or local anesthetic
Short duration, cooperation, and easy airway access
questions.explanation: Large series show failed neuraxial or regional anesthesia, inability to tolerate MAC, and hypoxia or airway obstruction as the most common conversion reasons.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which THREE changes during MAC should prompt serious consideration of conversion/escalation? (Select 3)
options: Persistent severe hypercapnia despite initial airway/ventilation maneuvers
Loss of reliable IV access when IV anesthesia/rescue drugs are required
A procedural change that substantially increases invasiveness/stimulation
A brief isolated BP decrease corrected immediately
questions.explanation: Triggers include hypercarbia, loss of IV access, procedural change, agitation, coughing, aspiration, altered mental status, refractory instability, and prolonged surgery.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Repeated coughing during MAC threatens procedural safety despite correction of obvious causes. What is the best interpretation?
options: More oxygen alone will reliably stop coughing
The current anesthetic technique may no longer permit safe completion and conversion should be considered
Deepening sedation indefinitely is always safer than conversion
questions.explanation: Coughing is a listed trigger for conversion because it can threaten the airway and the procedure.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient moves during a critical neural portion of surgery despite an otherwise adequate MAC plan. When is conversion appropriate?
options: Whenever the patient stops responding to voice
Only after SpO2 remains below 90% for 30 seconds
When movement or other conditions prevent the procedure from continuing safely under the current technique
Only after the scheduled end time is exceeded
questions.explanation: Conversion is indicated when the procedure cannot safely continue under MAC. Patient movement near neural structures is one example.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During propofol MAC, the patient becomes agitated, processed-EEG values rise, and the IV site is swollen and cool. What is the best immediate interpretation?
options: The patient needs a larger bolus through the same IV
The propofol concentration is too low
The IV has likely infiltrated, so drug delivery is unreliable and new access/anesthetic escalation is required
questions.explanation: A swollen, cool IV site plus loss of expected hypnotic effect suggests infiltration and unreliable intravenous delivery. Giving larger doses through the same catheter can worsen tissue exposure without restoring anesthesia, so new reliable access and an appropriate rescue or conversion plan are needed.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A stable MAC case tempts the anesthesia professional to focus on unrelated chart work. Which safety principle is most threatened?
options: Continuous vigilance for changing sedation depth, airway, ventilation, and hemodynamics
Delegating airway management to the proceduralist
questions.explanation: MAC requires continuous vigilance and readiness for airway control, even when the case seems stable.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Before MAC, what expectation about consciousness and recall should be discussed?
options: Complete unconsciousness and amnesia are guaranteed
The patient may be awake or intermittently aware and may remember portions of the procedure
Monitoring can stop once the patient is comfortable
questions.explanation: Patients should know they may be awake and remember parts of the procedure; promising full sleep sets up awareness complaints.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: After MAC, a patient complains, "I was supposed to be completely asleep." Which preoperative intervention most directly reduces this mismatch?
options: Promise deeper sedation if the patient becomes anxious
Give enough midazolam to guarantee amnesia
Explain the intended MAC experience, possible recall, and possibility of conversion to general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Mismatch between the planned anesthetic and patient expectations contributes to complaints of awareness. Setting expectations, including possible conversion, prevents this.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Why is it reasonable to mention possible sore throat even when MAC is planned?
options: Nasal oxygen routinely injures the pharynx
Unexpected conversion may require an airway device
questions.explanation: Conversion to GA may require an LMA or ETT, which can cause a sore throat; setting this expectation prevents complaints.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which TWO expectations are appropriate to discuss before MAC? (Select 2)
options: Brief discomfort or awareness may occur
The patient may need to follow instructions
Direct discharge from the procedure room is guaranteed
questions.explanation: Patients should know they may feel brief discomfort, may need to follow instructions, may remember parts, and may be converted to GA if needed.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During orthopedic MAC, a patient may intermittently hear conversation or procedural sounds. How should this be framed beforehand?
options: Hearing sounds or having periods of awareness can be normal under MAC and does not by itself indicate anesthetic failure
Any auditory recall proves awareness under general anesthesia
Hearing sounds means the regional block failed
questions.explanation: Patients under MAC may hear procedural sounds and wake intermittently; setting this expectation reduces distress.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, the patient obstructs and SpO2 falls to 84%. What is the immediate priority?
options: Open the airway and restore effective ventilation/oxygenation
Ask the proceduralist to finish before intervening
Wait for capnography to normalize spontaneously
questions.explanation: Airway obstruction is treated first by relieving it (jaw thrust, airway adjunct) and supporting ventilation.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient becomes agitated and moves during a critical portion of MAC. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore the movement if SpO2 is normal
Give a large propofol bolus before assessing ventilation
Rapidly assess reversible causes such as hypoxemia, pain, hypercapnia, or inadequate block and convert if safe completion is no longer possible
Use neuromuscular blockade without securing the airway
questions.explanation: Agitation is a trigger. Look for causes like hypoxia or pain and convert if the procedure cannot continue safely.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During emergency conversion from MAC, the video laryngoscope has no power and induction medications were never prepared. Which planning failure occurred?
options: Airway rescue can appropriately depend on equipment being retrieved after deterioration
Conversion equipment is required only after deep sedation occurs
Only ASA IV patients require a conversion plan
The conversion-to-general-anesthesia pathway was not made immediately executable before the case began
questions.explanation: A conversion-to-GA plan, including equipment and drugs, must be ready before starting MAC.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During EGD under MAC, vomiting occurs with suspected pulmonary aspiration and worsening oxygenation. What should this trigger?
options: Immediate airway/ventilation management and consideration of conversion to a secured airway/general anesthesia
Continuation of MAC because aspiration is unrelated to airway protection
Delay intervention until chest radiography is obtained
questions.explanation: Aspiration during MAC can rapidly produce airway contamination, hypoxemia, and impaired ventilation. Immediate priorities are suction and restoration of oxygenation and ventilation, with conversion to a secured airway/general anesthesia when needed to protect the lungs and permit safe continuation.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Three MAC patients differ: one has persistent ETCO2 65 mmHg despite airway maneuvers; one has mild preincision anxiety; one has a small isolated HR increase. Which finding most strongly supports escalation/conversion?
options: Persistent hypercapnia despite appropriate initial ventilatory support
questions.explanation: Persistent hypercapnia despite airway repositioning and initial ventilatory support indicates that ventilation remains inadequate despite rescue maneuvers. Unlike mild anxiety or a small isolated heart-rate change, this is a physiologic failure of the current MAC technique and should prompt active ventilatory support and escalation or conversion if it cannot be corrected.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A diagnostic laparoscopy unexpectedly becomes an open abdominal exploration. Why should the anesthetic plan be reassessed?
options: The procedural change eliminates aspiration risk
Opening the abdomen reduces anesthetic requirements
The new procedure may exceed the stimulation, duration, immobility, and airway requirements safely supported by the original MAC plan
MAC must always continue once started
questions.explanation: Conversion from laparoscopy to open exploration changes the expected intensity and duration of surgical stimulation and may increase requirements for analgesia, immobility, ventilation control, and airway protection. The anesthetic should therefore be reassessed rather than assuming the original MAC plan remains appropriate.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: After additional midazolam during MAC, a patient becomes more restless and disinhibited while ventilation begins to worsen. What is the best response?
options: Add neuromuscular blocker without securing the airway
Give progressively larger midazolam doses until immobile
Recognize possible paradoxical/disinhibitory or excessive sedative effect and avoid reflexively giving more benzodiazepine while reassessing airway and causes
questions.explanation: Restlessness after additional midazolam can reflect paradoxical disinhibition, excessive sedation with hypoxemia/hypercapnia, pain, or another cause. Worsening ventilation makes reflexively administering more benzodiazepine unsafe; airway and ventilation should be reassessed while the drug contribution and other causes are evaluated.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which THREE developments commonly lead to conversion from MAC to general anesthesia? (Select 3)
options: Inability to tolerate the procedure under MAC
questions.explanation: Common reasons for abandoning MAC include failure of the primary regional or neuraxial anesthetic, inability of the patient to tolerate the procedure safely, and respiratory compromise such as persistent hypoxemia or obstruction. Each represents failure of a condition required for safe continuation with the original technique.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A spinal anesthetic is inadequate during hip surgery and escalating sedation would be required to tolerate surgical pain. What is the safest next step?
options: Reassess the anesthetic and convert to a technique that reliably provides surgical anesthesia, including general anesthesia when appropriate
Continue escalating propofol until the patient no longer moves
Use paralysis without securing the airway
questions.explanation: Failed neuraxial anesthesia is a common reason for conversion. Adding sedation alone may lead to unsafe depth.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient was promised complete unconsciousness during MAC but later recalls portions of the procedure. Which problem most directly contributed to dissatisfaction?
options: Preoperative expectations did not match the intended anesthetic experience
The regional block must have failed
questions.explanation: MAC does not inherently guarantee continuous unconsciousness or complete amnesia. Promising those outcomes creates an expectation that the planned technique may not reliably meet, so otherwise acceptable intraoperative recall can be experienced as an anesthetic failure.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Two otherwise similar MAC patients receive different counseling: one is told partial awareness/recall may occur; the other is promised complete sleep. Which factor most increases the second patient's risk of dissatisfaction afterward?
options: The first patient will necessarily receive less sedative
questions.explanation: Recall can occur during MAC because the intended depth may permit responsiveness or awareness and amnesia is drug- and dose-dependent. A promise of complete sleep therefore creates a mismatch between the expected and intended anesthetic experience, increasing dissatisfaction if recall occurs.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, a patient becomes acutely confused, combative, and unable to cooperate. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore the change if SpO2 is normal
Assume the only cause is inadequate sedation
Give a large propofol bolus before assessing ventilation
Assess causes such as hypoxemia, hypercapnia, pain, drug effect, or neurologic change and escalate/convert if safe continuation is impossible
questions.explanation: Altered mental status that prevents safe continuation is a conversion trigger.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, severe hypotension and bradycardia persist despite appropriate initial treatment. What should be considered?
options: The current technique may no longer be safe; escalate resuscitation and consider conversion as clinically indicated
Continue unchanged until the procedure ends
questions.explanation: Hemodynamic instability is a trigger for conversion if it prevents safe continuation.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Why should a patient be told before MAC that they may need to follow commands?
options: Some procedures depend on cooperation, positioning, or neurologic assessment
All MAC patients must remain fully awake
questions.explanation: MAC often preserves enough responsiveness for purposeful interaction. Procedures may require the patient to cooperate with positioning, remain still on request, report symptoms, or participate in neurologic assessment, so this possibility should be explained before sedation.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During a quiet MAC, the anesthesia professional focuses on unrelated work and relies on alarms to regain attention. Which principle is violated?
options: Stable patients require observation only at induction and emergence
Documentation should occur only after the case
Continuous vigilance and readiness to intervene before deterioration reaches alarm thresholds
The proceduralist should monitor the airway
questions.explanation: Alarms are backup safety systems, not substitutes for continuous clinical observation. Sedation can progress rapidly from obstruction or hypoventilation to severe physiologic compromise, so continuous vigilance allows intervention before deterioration reaches an alarm threshold.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which preoperative statement most clearly requires correction before MAC?
options: "I was told I'll definitely be completely unconscious and remember nothing."
questions.explanation: MAC is an anesthesia service that may involve minimal through deep sedation, and neither complete unconsciousness nor amnesia is guaranteed. This statement signals a mismatch between the patient's expectation and the planned technique that should be corrected during informed discussion.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: When MAC unexpectedly requires conversion to general anesthesia, which resource must already be immediately accessible?
questions.explanation: Immediate availability of airway adjuncts and advanced airway equipment is required in the MAC environment.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which event during MAC is least likely, by itself, to justify conversion to general anesthesia?
options: Persistent coughing that prevents safe surgery
questions.explanation: Mild anxiety that resolves with reassurance does not represent failure of ventilation, airway protection, hemodynamic stability, analgesia, or procedural tolerance. Conversion is more strongly supported when the current technique can no longer safely meet those requirements.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Late in MAC, a patient repeatedly reaches toward the sterile field. What should happen before simply increasing sedation?
options: Give repeated propofol boluses until motion stops
Assess pain, hypoxemia/hypercapnia, positioning, bladder discomfort, anxiety, and procedural tolerance; convert if safe MAC is no longer feasible
Ignore the behavior if BP is normal
questions.explanation: Restlessness may reflect pain, position, or a full bladder, and more drug risks deeper-than-intended sedation. Reassess and be ready to convert.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient asks whether propofol MAC guarantees no memory. What is the most accurate response?
options: Any recall means the patient was never sedated
Propofol guarantees complete amnesia at every sedating dose
Recall varies with dose, adjuncts, and depth; portions of the procedure may be remembered
questions.explanation: Propofol can produce amnesia, but recall during MAC varies with dose, achieved depth, adjunct medications, and individual response. Because MAC does not require continuous unconsciousness, the patient should be told that portions of the procedure may be remembered.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A planned 1-hour MAC extends to 3 hours; the patient becomes restless, requires increasing propofol, and begins obstructing. What is the best interpretation?
options: Prolonged duration plus escalating sedation and obstruction indicate the original MAC plan may no longer be safe
More propofol is the only appropriate response
The problem is necessarily loss of IV access
questions.explanation: Increasing duration can produce discomfort and fatigue, but the key danger here is the escalating propofol requirement accompanied by recurrent obstruction. That combination shows that maintaining procedural tolerance is beginning to require a depth at which the unsecured airway is no longer reliably safe.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, RR is 6/min and ETCO2 remains 62 mmHg despite stimulation and airway repositioning; SpO2 is acceptable on oxygen. What should drive management?
options: Normal SpO2 proves ventilation is adequate
Persistent inadequate ventilation despite initial maneuvers, not the temporarily preserved SpO2
Hypercapnia is expected and needs no action
Increase oxygen flow without addressing ventilation
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen can maintain arterial saturation for a period despite severe hypoventilation, so an acceptable SpO2 does not establish adequate ventilation. A respiratory rate of 6/min with persistent ETCO2 elevation despite basic maneuvers indicates ongoing ventilatory failure that requires active support and possible escalation.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A procedure unexpectedly becomes substantially more invasive during MAC. What should be done?
options: Reassess whether the original anesthetic still provides adequate analgesia, immobility, physiologic control, and airway safety; convert if needed
questions.explanation: A more invasive procedure can abruptly change analgesic, immobility, duration, ventilation, and airway requirements. The anesthetic plan must be reassessed against those new demands, with conversion when MAC can no longer provide safe operating conditions.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Before MAC for a painful procedure, which discussion most directly prepares the patient for possible conversion of the anesthetic plan?
options: Avoid discussing conversion because it increases anxiety
Promise the patient will remain awake regardless of events
State that conversion is impossible once MAC begins
Explain that deeper sedation or general anesthesia may become necessary if comfort, immobility, airway patency, or procedural conditions cannot be maintained safely
questions.explanation: MAC requires a plan for rescue and possible conversion when the intended sedation level cannot safely meet procedural or patient needs. Discussing that possibility beforehand supports informed expectations and avoids presenting sedation depth as a guarantee.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A short outpatient procedure requires rapidly titratable hypnosis with fast onset and recovery, while local anesthesia supplies analgesia. Which IV agent best fits?
questions.explanation: Propofol is the most common MAC drug because of its rapid onset and offset and easy titration.

questions.stem: Propofol produces hypnosis primarily through which receptor action?
options: Positive modulation/potentiation of GABA-A receptor activity
questions.explanation: Propofol potentiates GABA-A receptor activity, producing hypnosis and amnesia. NMDA antagonism is ketamine and alpha-2 agonism is dexmedetomidine.

questions.stem: An elderly hypovolemic patient with poor cardiac reserve becomes profoundly hypotensive after a propofol bolus tolerated by a younger healthy adult. Why?
options: Propofol has active metabolites that accumulate only in older adults
Age, reduced reserve, volume depletion, and coadministered drugs can markedly increase propofol's hemodynamic effect
Injection pain directly causes prolonged hypotension
questions.explanation: Propofol decreases systemic vascular tone and can depress myocardial performance, while older age, hypovolemia, limited cardiac reserve, and synergistic coadministered sedatives reduce tolerance of those effects. A bolus acceptable in a young euvolemic patient can therefore cause disproportionate hypotension in a frail hypovolemic patient.

questions.stem: A patient is deeply hypnotized with propofol alone but still shows a marked response to incision. Which property explains this?
options: Propofol provides analgesia only at low doses
Propofol is not a primary analgesic
questions.explanation: Propofol is a hypnotic without analgesic properties, so painful stimulation still causes a response.

questions.stem: Which FOUR strategies can reduce propofol injection pain? (Select 4)
options: Use a larger proximal vein when possible
Pretreat with lidocaine using an effective technique
Administer through a well-running carrier IV
Inject rapidly into a small hand vein
questions.explanation: Propofol injection pain is reduced by decreasing the local concentration and endothelial exposure at the injection site or by pretreating the vein. A larger proximal vein, adequate carrier flow, slower injection, lidocaine with venous occlusion, and selected opioid pretreatment can all reduce discomfort.

questions.stem: Propofol causes severe burning through a small hand IV. Which change is most likely to reduce discomfort while maintaining IV administration?
options: Use a larger/proximal vein or well-running carrier and slow the injection, with lidocaine pretreatment when appropriate
Move to a smaller distal vein
questions.explanation: Slower injection into a fast-running line reduces pain. A larger antecubital vein or lidocaine pretreatment would also help.

questions.stem: Which pharmacokinetic characteristic makes propofol easy to titrate for brief sedation?
options: A very long fixed duration prevents fluctuations
Rapid onset and redistribution produce fast changes in clinical effect after dose adjustment
A specific reversal agent permits instant awakening
questions.explanation: Propofol reaches the brain quickly and its clinical effect changes rapidly after bolus or infusion adjustments because of rapid distribution and redistribution. This permits relatively prompt titration of hypnotic depth during short procedures.

questions.stem: Which THREE adverse effects should be anticipated after a large propofol bolus? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: A large propofol bolus can abruptly produce dose-dependent respiratory depression or apnea and hypotension from vasodilation with some myocardial depression. Injection pain is also common, whereas emergence reactions and hypersalivation are more characteristic of ketamine and chest-wall rigidity of potent opioids.

questions.stem: During intended moderate sedation, the patient becomes unresponsive to verbal commands and requires repeated airway maneuvers to maintain ventilation. What principle should guide management?
options: Airway support is unnecessary unless SpO2 reaches zero
The procedure must continue because the intended level was moderate
Sedation exists on a continuum, so the provider must rescue the patient from a deeper-than-intended level
The event automatically converts the case to general anesthesia billing
questions.explanation: Sedation depth can unintentionally progress beyond the intended level. The provider must recognize the actual clinical state and be capable of rescuing airway and ventilation while reducing or stopping sedative administration as appropriate.

questions.stem: Why may backup IV access be valuable during prolonged deep propofol anesthesia/sedation when the only existing IV is difficult to observe?
options: A second IV prevents injection pain
Loss or infiltration of the sole IV can abruptly interrupt hypnosis and delay delivery of rescue drugs
questions.explanation: Deep propofol cases depend on reliable IV access; losing the only IV can lead to awareness or delay rescue drugs.

questions.stem: An IV sedative has delayed onset and is followed by characteristic perineal paresthesia/pruritus. Which agent best fits?
questions.explanation: Fospropofol is a water-soluble prodrug; conversion to propofol delays onset, and perineal paresthesia and pruritus are typical side effects.

questions.stem: Compared with direct propofol administration, why is fospropofol onset slower?
options: It must undergo enzymatic conversion to active propofol
It is stored only in adipose tissue before activation
It requires renal conversion to midazolam
questions.explanation: Fospropofol must be converted to propofol, so onset is delayed and recovery is slower.

questions.stem: Perineal tingling and generalized pruritus without an allergic rash occur after administration of a propofol prodrug. Which agent is most likely?
questions.explanation: Perineal paresthesia and pruritus are characteristic of fospropofol.

questions.stem: Fospropofol was previously approved in the United States for monitored anesthesia care sedation but is no longer marketed. Which statement best reflects its current practical status?
options: It is the preferred U.S. ICU sedative
It is a first-line U.S. induction agent
It is approved only for neuromuscular blockade
It is not currently marketed for routine U.S. clinical use
questions.explanation: Fospropofol is a water-soluble prodrug of propofol that previously received U.S. approval for MAC sedation but was subsequently discontinued from the market. Its pharmacology remains testable, but it is not a routinely marketed U.S. clinical sedative.

questions.stem: Fospropofol was developed to provide which pharmacologic effect?
options: IV sedation after enzymatic conversion to propofol
questions.explanation: Fospropofol is a water-soluble prodrug converted to propofol and was developed as an IV sedative. Its historical regulatory status should be kept separate from its pharmacology.

questions.stem: Why does fospropofol produce less classic lipid-emulsion injection pain than propofol?
options: It is a water-soluble prodrug rather than the standard propofol lipid emulsion
questions.explanation: Standard propofol is formulated in a lipid emulsion and commonly causes pain on injection. Fospropofol is water soluble and does not use the same lipid formulation, so classic propofol injection pain is reduced, although fospropofol has its own characteristic paresthesia and pruritus.

questions.stem: A fospropofol sedation protocol proposes pulse oximetry alone with no airway-rescue equipment. What is the major flaw?
options: Conversion to active propofol can still produce clinically important respiratory depression, so ventilation monitoring and rescue capability remain necessary
Airway equipment is needed only for inhaled anesthetics
questions.explanation: Fospropofol can still cause respiratory depression and hypotension, so rescue capability and appropriate monitoring are required.

questions.stem: For a brief outpatient procedure requiring rapid titration and rapid recovery, which agent generally best fits among these choices?
questions.explanation: Propofol's rapid onset and relatively rapid offset make it well suited to short procedures requiring frequent depth adjustments and prompt recovery. Dexmedetomidine and fospropofol have slower onset, while midazolam may produce less predictable or prolonged recovery in susceptible patients.

questions.stem: A patient receives midazolam before propofol and becomes apneic after a smaller propofol dose than expected. Which principle best explains this?
options: Sedative drug interactions can be synergistic, reducing the propofol dose needed while increasing respiratory risk
questions.explanation: Midazolam and propofol both enhance inhibitory GABAergic effects, so coadministration can reduce the dose of propofol required for hypnosis while increasing respiratory depression beyond what either dose might cause alone. Dose requirements should therefore be reduced and titrated to effect when sedatives are combined.

questions.stem: Propofol provides adequate hypnosis and amnesia, but the patient still responds strongly to incision. Which anesthetic component is missing?
questions.explanation: Propofol provides hypnosis and amnesia without analgesia, so painful stimuli still cause responses.

questions.stem: A hypovolemic patient with active GI bleeding receives a standard propofol bolus and becomes profoundly hypotensive. Which mechanism contributes most?
options: Propofol-related vasodilation and myocardial depression are poorly tolerated when preload/reserve are already reduced
Hypovolemia prevents propofol from reaching the brain
questions.explanation: Propofol causes vasodilation and myocardial depression, which are exaggerated in hypovolemic patients.

questions.stem: Only a small peripheral IV is available and propofol injection pain is anticipated. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Use the smallest distal vein available
Use a well-running carrier, slower injection, and lidocaine pretreatment when appropriate
questions.explanation: Opioid pretreatment, lidocaine with venous occlusion, larger veins, slower injection, and a fast-running carrier all reduce propofol injection pain.

questions.stem: An 80-kg patient receives propofol at 100 mcg/kg/min from a 10 mg/mL solution. What pump rate is required?
questions.explanation: 100 mcg/kg/min × 80 kg = 8,000 mcg/min = 8 mg/min = 480 mg/hr. At 10 mg/mL, that is 48 mL/hr.

questions.stem: Why is loss of purposeful responsiveness during propofol sedation clinically important?
options: It may signal progression toward general-anesthesia depth with increasing risk of airway and ventilatory failure
It indicates propofol has stopped working
questions.explanation: Loss of purposeful response even to painful stimulation meets the responsiveness criterion for general-anesthesia depth rather than deep sedation. With propofol, this transition can occur quickly and is accompanied by increasing likelihood of airway intervention and inadequate spontaneous ventilation.

questions.stem: Which drug provides potent hypnosis but little or no intrinsic analgesia?
questions.explanation: Propofol provides no analgesia; ketamine and the opioids do.

questions.stem: A propofol infusion is running at 50 mcg/kg/min. The procedure becomes more stimulating and the patient begins purposeful movement without airway obstruction. Which response best reflects rational titration?
options: Ignore movement because propofol has a fixed effective dose
Immediately double the rate without reassessment
Give a neuromuscular blocker while maintaining the same sedation
Increase the infusion incrementally while reassessing responsiveness, ventilation, and hemodynamics
questions.explanation: Propofol should be titrated to clinical effect because stimulation, age, comorbidity, and coadministered drugs change dose requirements. Incremental adjustment with repeated assessment is safer than treating a calculated infusion rate as a fixed endpoint.

questions.stem: A patient with severe OSA requires cooperative sedation while preservation of spontaneous ventilation is especially important. Which agent may be advantageous because it causes relatively little respiratory depression?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine generally causes less respiratory depression than propofol, benzodiazepines, or opioids and can be useful when cooperative sedation and spontaneous ventilation are priorities. OSA still requires careful airway monitoring because no sedative eliminates obstruction risk.

questions.stem: For sedation in severe OSA, which dexmedetomidine tradeoff should be anticipated?
options: Less respiratory depression but slower onset and risk of bradycardia/hypotension
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine tends to preserve ventilation better than many sedatives, but onset can be slower and clinically important bradycardia and hypotension may occur, especially with loading doses or susceptible patients.

questions.stem: After a dexmedetomidine loading dose, marked bradycardia and hypotension develop without respiratory depression. Which explanation best fits?
questions.explanation: Bradycardia and hypotension are the key considerations with dexmedetomidine, along with slower onset.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient is ordered dexmedetomidine 1 mcg/kg over 10 minutes from a 4 mcg/mL solution. What pump rate delivers the loading dose?
questions.explanation: The load is 70 mcg, or 17.5 mL at 4 mcg/mL. Delivering 17.5 mL over 10 minutes requires 105 mL/hr.

questions.stem: A patient with renal dysfunction needs brief benzodiazepine sedation with rapid recovery. Which agent is rapidly hydrolyzed by carboxylesterase metabolism and has an inactive metabolite?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine hydrolyzed primarily by carboxylesterase 1 to a metabolite with very low pharmacologic activity. Renal impairment has relatively little effect on parent-drug disposition, although severe hepatic impairment can reduce clearance and prolong recovery.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes remimazolam disposition?
options: It is eliminated unchanged only by the kidneys
It is rapidly hydrolyzed by carboxylesterase 1 to a largely inactive metabolite
It requires CYP3A4 oxidation as its principal termination pathway
It has no clinically relevant effect from severe hepatic dysfunction
questions.explanation: Remimazolam undergoes rapid carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis, producing an inactive metabolite. Renal impairment has limited effect on the parent drug, whereas severe hepatic impairment can slow clearance and prolong recovery.

questions.stem: After remimazolam plus fentanyl, a patient is somnolent and hypoventilating. Which antagonist reverses the benzodiazepine component specifically?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is a benzodiazepine and is reversed by flumazenil; naloxone reverses the fentanyl component.

questions.stem: Which benzodiazepine best matches rapid titration and carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis when renal dysfunction is present?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is rapidly hydrolyzed by carboxylesterase 1 and can have a predictable short offset. Severe hepatic impairment can still prolong its effect, so it should not be described as completely organ-independent.

questions.stem: A frail patient with limited hemodynamic reserve requires brief benzodiazepine sedation and predictable recovery. Which option may offer less prolonged accumulation than conventional longer-acting benzodiazepines?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam's rapid carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis can limit prolonged accumulation and support predictable recovery compared with conventional longer-acting benzodiazepines. It can still cause hypotension and respiratory depression, especially with other depressants, so frailty still warrants careful titration.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about remimazolam are correct? (Select 2)
options: It acts at GABA-A receptors as a benzodiazepine
Its benzodiazepine effects can be antagonized by flumazenil
It depends primarily on renal excretion for termination
It has a long context-sensitive offset
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is a benzodiazepine positive modulator at GABA-A receptors and its sedative effect can be antagonized by flumazenil. It does not provide analgesia, and despite its short offset it can still produce respiratory depression, particularly with opioids.

questions.stem: Why can midazolam produce a less predictable or prolonged recovery than remimazolam in an older patient with organ dysfunction?
options: Remimazolam is stored in adipose tissue for days
Midazolam relies more on hepatic metabolism and can accumulate, whereas remimazolam undergoes rapid esterase metabolism
Midazolam is metabolized only by plasma esterases
questions.explanation: Midazolam depends substantially on hepatic CYP3A metabolism and has active metabolites whose effects can become prolonged in older or organ-impaired patients. Remimazolam is rapidly hydrolyzed by carboxylesterase 1, generally producing a shorter, more predictable offset, although severe hepatic impairment can still slow its clearance.

questions.stem: Small doses of midazolam and fentanyl together cause apnea. Which principle best explains this?
options: Benzodiazepine-opioid respiratory depression can be synergistic
The drugs prevent one another's metabolism completely
questions.explanation: Midazolam causes respiratory depression, especially with opioids. Sedatives and opioids have synergistic respiratory depression.

questions.stem: A hypotensive patient needs painful burn-dressing care while preserving spontaneous ventilation as much as possible. Which agent may be advantageous because it provides analgesia and sympathetic support?
questions.explanation: Ketamine provides both analgesia and dissociative sedation and usually stimulates sympathetic tone, tending to preserve blood pressure better than propofol in a patient with limited hemodynamic reserve. Spontaneous ventilation is often maintained, but apnea, obstruction, vomiting, secretions, and laryngospasm remain possible.

questions.stem: Which THREE effects are commonly associated with ketamine? (Select 3)
options: Increased heart rate/blood pressure in many patients
questions.explanation: Ketamine commonly produces sympathetic stimulation, increased salivation, and psychoperceptual emergence phenomena. Its relative preservation of spontaneous ventilation does not eliminate airway complications, including laryngospasm, so suction and airway rescue capability remain necessary.

questions.stem: A child continues breathing spontaneously after ketamine. Why must ventilation monitoring and airway-rescue capability still remain available?
options: Ketamine does not eliminate the risk of obstruction, apnea, vomiting, or laryngospasm
Preserved spontaneous breathing guarantees airway protection
questions.explanation: Ketamine preserves ventilation more often than propofol, but laryngospasm and other airway complications can still occur.

questions.stem: Why can ketamine plus propofol be useful for a brief painful procedure?
options: Propofol supplies the analgesia missing from ketamine
Ketamine contributes analgesia and sympathetic support while propofol contributes titratable hypnosis
Both agents reliably increase blood pressure
questions.explanation: The drugs complement rather than duplicate each other: ketamine supplies analgesia and sympathetic support, while propofol supplies rapidly titratable hypnosis and can blunt some ketamine-related emergence effects. The combination still requires careful titration because respiratory and hemodynamic complications remain possible.

questions.stem: A brief intensely painful stimulus requires an opioid that can be titrated rapidly and wears off quickly when stopped. Which choice best fits, with respiratory depression as the major tradeoff?
questions.explanation: Remifentanil is rapidly metabolized by nonspecific blood and tissue esterases, giving it a very short context-sensitive half-time and allowing rapid adjustment to brief painful stimulation. That same potency can cause abrupt respiratory depression or apnea, so ventilation must be closely monitored.

questions.stem: After a rapid large fentanyl bolus, bag-mask ventilation becomes difficult despite an open upper airway because the chest is rigid. What complication should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Rapid administration of a large fentanyl dose can cause marked truncal and chest-wall rigidity that makes ventilation difficult even when the upper airway is patent. Management centers on restoring ventilation, with opioid antagonism and/or neuromuscular blockade considered according to severity and the clinical setting.

questions.stem: During remifentanil sedation, RR falls to 6/min and ETCO2 rises. What is the immediate priority?
options: Reduce/stop opioid delivery as appropriate and support airway/ventilation
Wait because the short context-sensitive half-time prevents dangerous hypoventilation
questions.explanation: Remifentanil causes significant respiratory depression. Reduce the infusion and support ventilation.

questions.stem: During sedation, hypnosis is adequate but a brief painful stimulus still requires rapidly titratable analgesia. Which drug provides the analgesic component?
questions.explanation: Fentanyl provides rapid-onset analgesia and is useful for painful procedures.

questions.stem: Which FOUR agents provide clinically meaningful analgesia as part of a sedation technique? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Fentanyl and remifentanil are opioid analgesics, while ketamine provides substantial analgesia through NMDA-receptor antagonism; other analgesic adjuncts may also contribute depending on the listed choices. Propofol and benzodiazepines provide hypnosis, sedation, or amnesia but do not supply reliable procedural analgesia.

questions.stem: A patient has a severe history of distressing hallucinations during prior dissociative sedation. Which agent is least attractive if alternatives meet the procedural goals?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is associated with emergence reactions.

questions.stem: During cooperative sedation for carotid angiography, HR falls to 42/min shortly after starting the sedative. Which agent most strongly fits this adverse-effect profile?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine commonly causes bradycardia and hypotension. Ketamine tends to raise HR and BP.

questions.stem: Midazolam plus fentanyl provides complementary effects during procedural sedation. Which drug supplies the primary analgesia?
questions.explanation: Fentanyl provides analgesia; midazolam provides anxiolysis, sedation, and amnesia.

questions.stem: Significant renal dysfunction is present, but rapid titration, amnesia, and relatively predictable benzodiazepine recovery are desired. Which agent best fits?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam provides titratable benzodiazepine sedation and amnesia with rapid carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis. Severe hepatic impairment can prolong clearance, so renal dysfunction is the cleaner comparison here.

questions.stem: A patient remains excessively sedated after remimazolam. Which antagonist can reverse its benzodiazepine effect?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is a benzodiazepine and is reversible with flumazenil; the others have no flumazenil effect.

questions.stem: A dexmedetomidine loading infusion begins only a few minutes before the procedure, and the patient remains alert. Which property best explains the delayed effect?
options: The drug is inactive until hepatic conversion
Dexmedetomidine requires an opioid to produce any sedation
Dexmedetomidine generally has a slower onset than propofol
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine generally has a slower onset than propofol, so beginning a loading infusion only minutes before stimulation may not yet produce the desired sedative effect. This slower onset must be balanced against its advantage of relatively limited respiratory depression.

questions.stem: A cooperative sedation technique prioritizes preservation of spontaneous ventilation over rapid onset. Which agent may be advantageous?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine produces cooperative sedation through central alpha-2 agonism and usually depresses ventilation less than propofol, benzodiazepine-opioid combinations, or potent opioids. Its slower onset and potential for bradycardia and hypotension remain important tradeoffs.

questions.stem: After ketamine, copious oral secretions complicate airway management. Which drug effect is responsible?
questions.explanation: Ketamine can increase salivary and tracheobronchial secretions rather than suppress them. Copious secretions can obstruct visualization and contribute to airway irritation, so suction and airway-rescue readiness are important.

questions.stem: Which sedative-analgesic produces dissociation primarily through NMDA-receptor antagonism?
questions.explanation: Ketamine primarily antagonizes NMDA glutamate receptors, producing a dissociative state with both sedation and analgesia. This distinguishes it from GABAergic hypnotics such as propofol and benzodiazepines, which do not provide comparable intrinsic analgesia.
